chunks: And Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr al-Bazanti narrated from Abd al-Karim ibn Amr from Abu Basir from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

The curse (l'an) does not take effect until the man enters with his wife, and the curse does not occur except by denying the child. Therefore, there is no contradiction between these two reports and the first two reports, because the first two reports are consistent with the apparent meaning of the Quran. Allah the Exalted said: 'And those who accuse their wives and have no witnesses except themselves...' The verse did not stipulate the denial of the child in that matter, so it must be established in every place where the accusation occurred. And the first two reports also confirm this, with the fact that the first of the last two reports, if the intended meaning was the removal of the curse merely by the accusation in all cases, would be contradictory because he said 'The curse does not occur except by denying the child,' then he said 'And when the man accuses the woman, he curses her.' If the intended meaning was what some people went to, it would be contradictory as you see. The solution in these two reports is that the curse in the accusation does not occur merely by the accusation until he adds to that the claim of witnessing (consummation), and the ruling of denying the child is not like that, because whenever the child is denied, the curse becomes obligatory upon him even if he did not claim witnessing of the illicit act. Thus, the two rulings differ in denying the child and mere accusation from this aspect, and that which indicates that witnessing is a condition in the accusation...
ai.seo_question: What are the conditions for the Islamic curse (l'an) to take effect between husband and wife?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi uses this narration to harmonize apparent contradictions in hadith by distinguishing between the general accusation (qadhf) and the specific legal procedure of l'an, which requires both denial of offspring and a claim of witnessing the act. This distinction ensures consistency with the Quranic text in Surah An-Nur, where the curse is triggered by the accusation itself, while the hadith clarifies the procedural prerequisites for its validity in Shia jurisprudence. The scholar emphasizes that the denial of lineage is the core condition, whereas the claim of witnessing serves to substantiate the specific nature of the accusation.
